item.title: Early adequate empiric antifungal therapy and 28-day mortality in ICU patients with candidemia: a pooled patient-level analysis of EUROBACT-1 and EUROBACT-2 cohorts
item.description:
Background: The optimal timing of empiric antifungal therapy in patients with suspected candidemia remains uncertain. In practice, many antifungal treatments initiated empirically are eventually found to be unnecessary, exposing patients to potential toxicity, selection of non-albicans Candida species, emergence of resistance, and additional costs. The objective of the study was to evaluate whether adequate empiric antifungal therapy initiated within 2 days after blood culture draw was associated with 28-day mortality.

Methods: We performed a pooled secondary analysis of two prospective worldwide observational cohorts (EUROBACT-1 and EUROBACT-2) including adult patients with Candida bloodstream infection. The exposure was defined as receipt of adequate antifungal therapy within 2 days after blood culture draw. Propensity scores for receiving early adequate antifungal therapy were estimated using prespecified covariates, and inverse probability of treatment weights were applied in a weighted Cox proportional hazards model to assess the association with 28-day mortality. Prespecified subgroup analyses were conducted according to study cohort, Candida species, and presence of hypotension at the time of bloodstream infection. As a sensitivity analysis, a frailty Cox proportional hazards model including a random center effect was performed.

Results: The final study population included 272 patients with candidemia from 158 centers, including 81 from EUROBACT-1 and 191 from EUROBACT-2. One hundred and ten patients received early adequate antifungal therapy and 162 did not. Overall, 38.6% of patients (105/272) died within 28 days, including 40.9% (45/110) in the early adequate therapy group and 37.0% (60/162) in the non-early adequate therapy group. In the weighted Cox model, early adequate antifungal therapy was not significantly associated with 28-day mortality (HR 1.23, 95% CI 0.82-1.83, p = 0.314). Results were consistent across subgroup analyses according to study cohort, Candida species, the presence of hypotension at the time of bloodstream infection, as well as in the frailty Cox sensitivity analysis.

Conclusions: Early adequate antifungal therapy was not independently associated with improved 28-day survival in ICU patients with candidemia. These findings support a more targeted approach to early empirical antifungal treatment and underscore the need to identify patient subgroups most likely to benefit from immediate therapy.

item.title: Treatment and outcomes of difficult-to-treat Stenotrophomonas maltophilia pneumonia in the intensive care unit: a multinational retrospective cohort study
item.description:
Objectives: Difficult-to-treat resistance (DTR) in Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is an emerging concern in ICU-acquired pneumonia, associated with high mortality and limited evidence to guide therapy. This study aimed to evaluate the association between antibiotic regimens and 30-day mortality in DTR S. maltophilia ICU-acquired pneumonia.

Methods: We conducted a multicenter, international, retrospective study across 31 centers in eight countries, including all adult patients with DTR S. maltophilia ICU-acquired pneumonia treated with ≥24 hours of an in vitro-active antibiotic. The primary outcome was 30-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included clinical cure and a composite of 30-day survival with clinical cure. Each agent was analyzed as a separate exposure using modified Poisson regression with robust variance in a day-3 landmark cohort. Combination therapy and treatment duration were evaluated using overlap weighting.

Results: A total of 119 patients were included. Thirty-day mortality was 37.8%. Tigecycline was associated with higher 30-day mortality (aRR 1.95, 95% CI 1.21-3.13). Aztreonam/ceftazidime-avibactam showed a favorable but non-significant trend toward lower mortality (aRR 0.38, 95% CI 0.12-1.15), as did colistin (aRR 0.51, 95% CI 0.22-1.20). No agent other than tigecycline was significantly associated with any outcome, and the active agents had wide, overlapping confidence intervals. Neither combination therapy nor a treatment duration longer than 8 days was associated with any outcome.

Conclusions: Tigecycline was associated with excess mortality and should be used with caution. Aztreonam/ceftazidime-avibactam and colistin trended toward lower mortality, whereas the other agents, including cefiderocol, appeared neutral. The study is underpowered to separate the active agents, and these hypothesis-generating findings require prospective confirmation.

item.title: Physiological determinants of piperacillin and cefazolin clearance in septic and trauma patients
item.description:
Background: Physiological alterations in patients with sepsis and trauma can influence antibiotic clearance, yet reliable predictors remain poorly defined. We aimed to investigate the determinants of piperacillin and cefazolin clearance in these populations to identify bedside indicators of subtherapeutic exposure.

Methods: Prospective physiological and pharmacokinetic study in patients receiving piperacillin/tazobactam for sepsis or prophylactic cefazolin post-trauma. Patients also received intravenous sinistrin. Intensive pharmacokinetic sampling, cardiac output (CO) monitoring and four urinary creatinine clearance (uCLCR) measurements were performed. Data were analysed with non-compartmental pharmacokinetic methods, and linear and logistic regression.

Results: We enrolled 49 septic and 28 trauma patients. Trauma patients were younger (33.5 vs. 46.5 years) and had higher uCLCR (155.5 vs. 107.5 mL/min). Linear regression identified that lower Sequential Organ Failure Assessment scores and an hyperdynamic state with higher CO and 2 and 8-h uCLCR were the strongest predictors of increased piperacillin total clearance; higher 2-h uCLCR and hypoalbuminemia were the main predictors for cefazolin total clearance. Sinistrin CL was a weak predictor. Logistic regression identified augmented renal clearance (8-h uCLCR > 130 mL/min) as the main risk factor for piperacillin subtherapeutic exposure (OR 10.9, p < 0.05), also when defined using the Cockcroft-Gault cut-off of 114.5 mL/min from ROC analysis.

Conclusions: In sepsis, low sickness severity and a hyperdynamic state with high cardiac output lead to increased uCLCR and high piperacillin clearance. In trauma, high cefazolin clearance occurs in the presence of an elevated uCLCR and hypoalbuminemia. These bedside physiological indicators, along with Cockcroft-Gault CLCR, may serve as early indicators of risk for subtherapeutic exposure.

item.title: Assessing vascular barrier permeability in critically ill patients: what are we really measuring?
item.description:
Background: Perturbation of vascular barrier permeability is a central mechanism in the pathophysiology of critical illness, contributing to tissue edema, impaired oxygen diffusion, and organ dysfunction. Despite advances in the field, direct bedside assessment of vascular permeability remains unavailable. Current approaches rely on indirect and compartment-specific surrogates, raising important questions about what is actually being measured.

Main body: This narrative review summarizes the physiological principles underlying vascular barrier function and its disruption in conditions such as sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and major surgery. Currently available bedside tools used to assess vascular permeability or its consequences are critically appraised, including clinical examination, ultrasonography, transpulmonary thermodilution, bioelectrical impedance analysis, circulating biomarkers of endothelial injury (e.g., glycocalyx degradation products, angiopoietin-2), and albumin kinetics-based methods. While these techniques provide valuable insights, they predominantly reflect downstream consequences such as tissue edema, intravascular volume shifts, or endothelial activation rather than permeability itself. In addition, vascular permeability is a dynamic, context-dependent, and organ-specific process influenced by inflammatory, hemodynamic, and therapeutic factors, further complicating its interpretation. Each method therefore captures only a partial dimension of vascular barrier dysfunction, with important limitations related to specificity, feasibility, validation and standardization.

Conclusions: No single bedside tool currently provides a comprehensive assessment of vascular permeability in critically ill patients. A multimodal approach integrating clinical evaluation, imaging, hemodynamic monitoring, and biomarkers is required to better characterize vascular barrier dysfunction. Future research should focus on validating composite indices and developing reliable, real-time bedside tools capable of directly assessing vascular permeability, with the ultimate goal of improving risk stratification and guiding personalized therapeutic strategies.

item.title: Time-varying dose decisions in CRRT: why marginal structural and baseline Cox estimates should not be pooled
Eleven questions on Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome management in the ICU
item.description:
Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) due to Andes virus (ANDV) is a fulminant yet potentially reversible cause of respiratory and circulatory failure requiring timely critical care. This article addresses eleven practical questions on ICU management, drawing on clinical experience and research from the Chilean healthcare system. The recommendations cover early recognition, diagnostic workup, haemodynamic monitoring, cautious fluid and vasoactive support, respiratory management, VA-ECMO referral, daily ICU care, recovery, common pitfalls, and therapies with limited evidence. Because no antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy has consistently improved outcomes, survival relies on early suspicion, physiology-guided supportive care, and rapid escalation to ECMO-capable centres when severe cardiopulmonary failure develops.

item.title: Harmonizing the diagnosis of citrate accumulation - a call for standardized criteria
item.description:
Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) has emerged as the gold-standard strategy for continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), yet its widespread adoption remains hindered by perceived complexity, heterogeneous protocols, unclear contraindications, and inconsistent terminology. A central challenge lies in the recognition and management of citrate accumulation, for which no single, reliable biomarker exists. The total-to-ionized calcium (tCa/iCa) ratio is widely utilized as a sensitive surrogate, but its specificity is limited by multiple confounding factors, including serum albumin concentration, acid-base status, and exogenous calcium administration. Current evidence supports a paradigm shift from reliance on static thresholds toward a dynamic, physiology-based assessment to define citrate accumulation. The kinetics of the tCa/iCa ratio, when interpreted alongside evolving metabolic parameters, particularly lactate trends, systemic ionized calcium, and acid-base status, provide a more robust framework for identifying citrate accumulation. Crucially, an elevated tCa/iCa ratio should not indiscriminately prompt the discontinuation of RCA. Targeted adjustments to the CRRT prescription can often safely mitigate citrate burden while preserving circuit patency. In the absence of a validated and widely available method for the direct measurement of plasma citrate levels, we propose a stepwise approach incorporating routinely measured screening tools and confirmatory parameters. Studies incorporating direct plasma citrate concentration measurements should be conducted to validate these criteria alongside readily available bedside surrogate markers. Refining this framework is essential to enhance the safe implementation of RCA and ultimately improve outcomes in critically ill patients.

item.title: Coagulopathy and anticoagulation management in adult ECPR patients
item.description:
Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) has emerged as a lifesaving strategy for refractory cardiac arrest, restoring systemic perfusion when conventional cardiopulmonary resuscitation fails. However, ECPR profoundly disrupts haemostasis, driven by the combined effects of whole-body ischaemia-reperfusion injury, systemic inflammation, endothelial activation, platelet dysfunction, and blood contact with extracorporeal surfaces. Together, these processes create a highly dynamic and unstable thromboinflammatory milieu, marked by the simultaneous risk of thrombosis and life-threatening bleeding. Systemic anticoagulation is required to maintain circuit patency and prevent thromboembolic complications, yet optimal strategies remain uncertain. Haemostasis during ECPR is highly dynamic, shaped by the underlying aetiology of cardiac arrest, patient-specific characteristics, and circuit-related factors. This complexity underscores the limitations of fixed anticoagulation targets and the need for individualized, context-sensitive management guided by continuous clinical and laboratory assessment. Despite the increasing global adoption of ECPR, high-quality evidence to guide anticoagulation practices remains scarce. Current strategies are largely extrapolated from other extracorporeal life support populations, contributing to substantial inter-centre variability. This review synthesizes the available evidence on coagulopathy and anticoagulation in adult patients receiving ECPR and discusses emerging approaches to monitoring and anticoagulation management.

item.title: Distinct transcriptomic signatures discriminate hyperinflammation from immune paralysis in sepsis: a single-cell RNA sequencing study
item.description:
Background: Sepsis is a highly heterogeneous syndrome characterized by variable immune dysregulation states, including hyperinflammation and immunosuppression. Previous immunotherapy attempts in sepsis have largely failed, likely due to a "one-size-fits-all" approach that ignores each patient's immune status. The recent ImmunoSep randomized clinical trial demonstrated that precision immunotherapy guided by the presence of either macrophage activation-like syndrome (MALS) or immune paralysis can improve early organ dysfunction in sepsis patients. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying these immune endotypes remain unclear.

Objectives: To identify the immunological signatures that distinguish MALS and immune paralysis.

Methods: We used single-cell RNA sequencing to profile circulating leukocytes of 6 healthy controls and 16 sepsis patients classified as MALS, immune paralysis or unclassified (when criteria for neither of these two immune endotypes were applicable). Classification was based on surrogate biomarkers ferritin and HLA-DR expression on monocytes. Thereafter, the transcriptional programs of these groups were compared.

Results: Pronounced differences were detected mainly in the transcriptional signature of monocytes from these patients, with a clear distinction between MALS and immune paralysis. Unsupervised clustering analysis revealed the existence of MALS-specific monocyte clusters, as well as one sepsis-specific monocyte cluster that was linked to greater comorbidity burden and may reflect increased clinical vulnerability in sepsis. These findings were validated in two independent cohorts, in which urosepsis was characterized by heterogeneous MALS and immune paralysis monocyte signatures. Moreover, MALS-specific monocyte clusters showed overlapping transcriptional signatures with severe COVID-19.

Conclusions: Our findings shed light on the heterogeneous immune landscape underlying sepsis and provide opportunities for patient stratification for future therapeutic development.

item.title: Differentiated effect of hypothermia versus normothermia after cardiac arrest by neurological status and clinical correlates of ischemic burden
item.description:
Introduction: The optimal temperature target after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains uncertain, as major randomized trials have not demonstrated a clear benefit of lower-target hypothermia compared with normothermia. Despite this, patients with differing degrees of ischemic burden or early neurological injury may hypothetically respond differently to temperature targets, raising the possibility of heterogeneous treatment effects. This study aimed to determine whether outcomes differ after OHCA with 33 °C versus controlled normothermia (36.0-37.7 °C) according to correlates of ischemic burden and neurological findings at hospital admission.

Methods: This secondary analysis of the TTM and TTM2 trials employed effect-based machine learning to probe for heterogeneous treatment effects. Causal forests and Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) estimated individualized treatment effects (ITE) based on ischemia duration, prehospital factors, and neurological examination findings at hospital admission. Treatment effect modifier variable importance parameter (TEM-VIP) analysis ranked the baseline variables most likely to modify effect. The primary outcome was six-month all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was poor functional outcome (modified Rankin scale score 4-6). Primary analyses evaluated potential heterogeneity within each trial, while secondary analyses pooled all participants.

Measurements and main results: All 2789 adult OHCA patients from the trials' primary analyses were included (median age 65 years (IQR 56-73), 79.9% male). Death occurred in 49.4% of patients in the 33 °C group, and in 47.9% in the controlled normothermia group. Variation in six-month mortality ITEs estimated from ischemic burden correlates and initial neurological findings was minimal, and no significant heterogeneity of treatment effect was identified across all methods and analysis populations. In the pooled analysis, estimated conditional mean mortality risk difference ranged from - 1.2% to 2.1% in causal forest (p = 0.99), and from - 0.5% to 1.5% in BART, with posterior probabilities for hypothermia benefit ranging from 42% to 53%. Absolute subgroup estimates in TEM-VIP analysis were small and non-significant. Results were consistent for the six-month functional outcome.

Conclusions: Among TTM and TTM2 participants randomized to 33 °C versus controlled normothermia post-OHCA, no evidence of detectable heterogeneity of treatment effect based on available clinical correlates of ischemic burden or initial neurological findings was identified, with minimal estimated variation in treatment effect.

item.title: Accelerating tracheostomy decannulation with intermittent oro-esophageal feeding in neurogenic dysphagia: a multicenter randomized controlled trial
item.description:
Background: Neurogenic dysphagia frequently constitutes a major barrier to decannulation for tracheostomized patients. Conventional nasogastric tube (NGT) feeding may promote disuse atrophy of swallowing musculature and persistent aspiration risk. Intermittent oro-esophageal tube (IOE) feeding, a physiologically oriented modality mimicking natural swallowing, may accelerate decannulation, yet high-quality evidence is lacking.

Methods: In this multicenter randomized controlled trial conducted at three tertiary academic centers in China, tracheostomized adults with neurogenic dysphagia were randomly assigned 1:1 to IOE or NGT. All participants received standardized pharmacological treatment, pulmonary rehabilitation, and structured swallowing training, and entered an institutional decannulation protocol with predefined readiness criteria. The primary outcome was time from protocol entry to actual decannulation. Secondary outcomes included the 30-day successful decannulation rate, nutritional indices, swallowing function, and swallowing-related quality of life. Outcome assessors and statisticians were blinded to allocation. Analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle.

Results: A total of 140 patients were randomized to IOE (n = 70) or NGT (n = 70). Time to decannulation was shorter with IOE (22.16 ± 1.86 vs. 26.33 ± 1.30 days; between-group difference, 4.17 days; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.90-6.44; p < 0.001; log-rank p = 0.005). The 30-day successful decannulation rate was higher with IOE (65.71% vs. 47.14%; absolute difference, 18.57% points; 95% CI, 2.43-34.71; p = 0.028). At 1 month, the IOE group demonstrated greater improvements in body mass index, serum albumin, serum prealbumin, swallowing function, and swallowing-related quality of life (all p < 0.001). Pharyngeal discomfort was less frequent with IOE (14.06% vs. 34.21%; p = 0.006); no Grade Ⅲ or higher adverse events occurred.

Conclusions: Intermittent oro-esophageal tube feeding shortens time to decannulation and improves nutritional, swallowing, and quality-of-life outcomes compared with nasogastric tube feeding in tracheostomized patients with neurogenic dysphagia.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06791590, registration date January 19, 2025.

item.title: Understanding cerebral autoregulation and cerebrovascular reactivity: mechanistic perspectives and clinical insights from TBI
item.description:
Cerebrovascular reactivity and cerebral blood flow autoregulation are critical determinants of brain homeostasis but are often conflated in clinical practice. Although these constructs are closely related and arise from vascular responses to vasoactive stimuli, they reflect distinct physiological responses and measurement approaches: autoregulation is assessed through changes in cerebral blood flow, and pressure reactivity through changes in cerebral blood volume. A fundamental clinical challenge is that the full autoregulatory curve is rarely observable in an individual patient at a single point in time; consequently, isolated measurements from classical assessments or continuous indices such as the pressure reactivity index (PRx), mean flow index (Mx), and arterial mean flow index (Mxa) are each associated with different components of cerebrovascular physiology, providing only partial views of cerebrovascular function and frequently yielding apparently conflicting results. This Review addresses a central clinical question: can multimodal neuromonitoring help determine where a patient is operating on the autoregulatory curve? We synthesise current understanding of the physiological relationships among cerebral perfusion pressure, cerebral blood flow, and cerebral blood volume, and examine the mechanisms underlying divergent autoregulatory index behaviour. By integrating mechanistic physiological schematics and representative clinical cases, we propose an objective educational framework that links classical cerebrovascular physiology with contemporary bedside monitoring. Within this framework, six conceptual physiological zones are delineated. These zones demonstrate how variations in vascular tone, intracranial compliance, and critical closing pressure shape autoregulatory responses generate differing patterns in PRx, Mx, and Mxa. Fully defining a patient's complex cerebrovascular state requires looking beyond any single parameter. Together, PRx, Mx, and Mxa provide complementary information, where discordant findings may represent distinct physiological mechanisms rather than measurement error. Interpreting these indices together within a mechanistic framework may improve identification of a patient's position along the autoregulatory curve, support more consistent bedside interpretation, and ultimately facilitate personalised cerebral perfusion pressure management.
